title: Neuropathic and diabetic foot ulcers
summary: Painless ulcers on plantar pressure points surrounded by callus, from loss of protective sensation. Any diabetic foot ulcer needs referral to the foot care service within 1 working day (NICE NG19).

what: A **neuropathic ulcer** follows loss of **protective sensation**, with or without deformity and ischaemia (‘neuro-ischaemic’ foot). Most are **diabetic foot ulcers**, a leading cause of amputation.
cause: Peripheral neuropathy (usually diabetes; also alcohol, B12 deficiency, leprosy) means repetitive trauma goes unnoticed. Deep ulcers can reach bone, with a risk of **osteomyelitis**.

list: Site: **plantar** metatarsal heads, heel, tips of toes, under bunions.
Deep, punched-out, surrounded by **callus**; may reach bone.
Often **painless**; warm foot with good pulses (unless neuro-ischaemic).
Clawed toes, Charcot deformity, dry fissured skin.
Test sensation with a **10 g monofilament** and vibration.
**Probe to bone**, plus X-ray or MRI if osteomyelitis is suspected.
Deep tissue samples rather than surface swabs if infected.

differentials: [Arterial ulcer](condition:arterial-leg-ulcer), pressure ulcer (immobile or paraplegic patients), [venous ulcer](condition:venous-leg-ulcer), malignancy (non-healing).

list: **Any diabetic foot ulcer:** refer urgently to the **multidisciplinary foot care service** or foot protection service (within 1 working day, NICE NG19).
**Offloading**, glycaemic optimisation, debridement, and assessment for infection, which may need admission and IV antibiotics.
Diabetic foot infection: follow NICE NG19 and local antimicrobial guidance.

red_flags: Diabetic foot with **spreading redness, fever, crepitus or wet necrosis**: **ED / same-day admission**.
Probe to bone, or suspected osteomyelitis or **Charcot foot** (hot, swollen foot in neuropathy).
**Never ignore a ‘small’ plantar ulcer in diabetes.**
pearls: Teach **daily foot checks**, sensible footwear and podiatry follow-up; never walk barefoot with neuropathy.
Painless ulcer under a callus suggests neuropathic.
